about: The exhibit's leaves, in order: where the visitor stands (a station in render/stations.json), in which era and moment, looking which way (degrees), how the leaf arrives from the one before, and the words spoken, cut from docs/script.md with every word of a chapter kept in order. The player, the render queue (scripts/exhibit_queue.py) and the narration are all built from this file. Plan: docs/exhibit-2026-10.md.

leaves.say: This is Giza at dawn, from the rooftops of Nazlet el-Samman.
The Sphinx faces the sunrise, as it has for at least four and a half thousand years.
Behind it stand the pyramids of Khufu and Khafre.
The textbooks say Khafre's workmen carved the Sphinx about 2500 BCE.
Graham Hancock and Robert Bauval say the Sphinx and the plan of this plateau go back to about 10,500 BCE.
Robert Schoch, a geologist, says the rock agrees with them.
So how old is the Sphinx?
This piece makes their case as strongly as it can be made, and gives the archaeologists their answer.
It starts where Schoch did, with the walls of the ditch.
The Sphinx was not built. It was carved, by cutting a ditch around a knoll of bedrock, so the walls of the ditch are as old as the statue.
Robert Schoch, a geologist, looked at these walls in the early 1990s and saw rain.
The profile rolls. Harder beds stand out and softer beds are cut back into deep coves.
Vertical fissures open widest at the top, where water off the plateau would run in.
Wind and blown sand, he says, cut sharp level grooves instead, like those on the Old Kingdom tombs nearby.
Even Colin Reader, a geologist who rejects Schoch's date, agrees that running water cut these walls.
Then Schoch looked under the floor.
In a seismic survey published in 1992, he and a colleague sent sound through the rock.
By his account, the stone in front of the Sphinx and along its sides is weathered about two metres deep, and behind it only a little over one.
Deeper weathering means longer exposure, he argues, so the front was cut long before the back.
On his most cautious reckoning, the core of the Sphinx is at least seven thousand years old.
His own view now is the end of the last Ice Age, about 10,000 BCE.
If the body is that old, look again at the head.
Look at the head.
It wears the striped headcloth of a Fourth Dynasty king, and it is better kept than the body below it.
Beside that long body it is too small. Nobody disputes either point.
Hancock, Bauval and Schoch read the two facts as one story.
The figure was a lion first.
It stood through the long rains, and its head wore away.
When a king of the pyramid age took it over, his sculptors cut a royal face into what was left.
You can only carve a smaller form inside a larger one, so the new head came out small.
Here the king's head sits inside the lion's, and the ghost around it is the stone they cut away.
Even Colin Reader, who dates the Sphinx far later than they do, argued in 2026 that it began as a lion.
At the spring equinox the sun rises close to due east in every age, so the Sphinx's eastward gaze alone dates nothing.
But the stars behind the sunrise drift.
In about 10,500 BCE, Hancock and Bauval calculate, the constellation of the Lion rose in the east just before the equinox sun.
The lion on the ground watched its own image come up.
If the lion is that old, they argue, so are the temples at its feet.
At the Sphinx's paws stand two temples.
One of them, the Valley Temple, is lined with red granite from Aswan.
Behind the granite is a core of local limestone, in blocks that Flinders Petrie found ranging in weight to over a hundred tons each.
Those blocks came out of the Sphinx's own ditch, layer by layer. On that, the archaeologists and their critics agree.
The temples are built of the lion's stone, cut as the lion was freed from the rock.

Schoch and the writer John Anthony West went further. On camera in 1993, they said the limestone behind the granite is rounded and fissured like the ditch walls, and that the backs of the granite blocks were cut to fit that worn surface.
Schoch writes that the core blocks of both temples carry the weathering of heavy rain beneath their Old Kingdom granite. Nobody weathers a wall and then cases it.
On this reading the granite is a refit, laid over a building that was already old.
Hancock argues that the temple is credited to Khafre "on no good grounds whatsoever".
Khafre's statues, found inside it, and its granite show that he used and refaced the building. They leave the age of its core open.
And the Egyptians' own records put long ages before their first king.
Egypt did not think it began with its first king.
A papyrus in Turin, copied about 1250 BCE, lists the kings back to Menes, and before him gods, then spirits, then the Followers of Horus.
In the most probable reading of its damaged numbers, it gives the spirits and Followers 13,420 years and, in the next line, 23,200.
Manetho, a thousand years later, tells the same story.
The Egyptians called the beginning sep tepi, the First Time. Hancock and Bauval read it as a memory, not a myth: a golden age, they write, that immediately followed creation.
Here is the plateau as they picture it. The lion and its two temples stand alone.
Where the pyramids will rise, nothing stands yet.
A stela found beside the Great Pyramid says Khufu found a house of Isis "beside the house of the Sphinx". If that is true, they argue, the Sphinx was there before Khafre.
On the walls of King Unas's burial chambers at Saqqara, carved about 2400 BCE, the oldest copy of the Pyramid Texts sends the king into the sky. "Unas appears as a star."
"Orion is encircled by the Duat," it says, and so are Sothis, the star we call Sirius, and Unas.
None of these texts gives a date. Hancock and Bauval look for one in the sky.
In 1989 Robert Bauval argued that the three pyramids of Giza are laid out like the three stars of Orion's belt.
Two are nearly equal and stand on a diagonal. The third is smaller and set off the line, as Mintaka, the faintest, is.
To the Egyptians Orion was Sah, Osiris among the stars.
A study published in 2026 tested the pyramids' triangle against almost seven hundred thousand triplets of bright stars. It ranks in the top quarter of one per cent.
Every closer match is a group nobody ever named; Orion's belt is the first that someone did.
Bauval and Hancock take the plan as a clock.
Over twenty-six thousand years the wobble of the Earth's axis raises and lowers the belt on the southern meridian.
Drag the sky back.
The belt sinks until, about 10,500 BCE, it reaches the bottom of its swing.
That, they say, is the First Time, and the moment the plan records.
Inside the Great Pyramid, a shaft from the King's Chamber climbs south at 45 degrees.
In about 2450 BCE, Alnitak, the belt's easternmost star, crossed the meridian within a fifth of a degree of that line.
On their reading the stone holds two dates: when it was built, and when its plan was drawn.
They find numbers in it as well.
Measure the Great Pyramid. Walk once round its base and divide the distance by its original height.
The answer is two times pi, to within three hundredths of one per cent.
Draw a line from the apex down the middle of one face. Divide it by half the base and you get the golden ratio, within a twentieth of one per cent.
Scale the pyramid up 43,200 times. Its height becomes the distance from the Earth's centre to the pole, and its perimeter the equator, each within one per cent.
Graham Hancock points out that 43,200 is 600 times 72, and that 72 years is about how long the stars take to drift one degree.
The sides run within four minutes of arc of true north. On a side of 230 metres that is a quarter of a metre, with no compass.
Writers since Charles Piazzi Smyth in the 1860s have read these numbers as a design brief: the circle, the golden section, the size of the Earth and the slow turn of the sky, written into one shape.
For Hancock, the knowledge was inherited from a civilisation older than Egypt. Each number alone has an ordinary explanation.
Their own papyri teach the seked as a schoolroom exercise, but they were written centuries after the pyramids; no mathematics survives from the pyramid age itself.
The proponents ask whether the explanations hold when the numbers come together.
Knowledge that old needs people to have held it.
About 12,900 years ago, as the last Ice Age was ending, the warming stopped. For more than a thousand years the northern world fell back into cold.
Geologists call it the Younger Dryas. Hancock cites about a hundred peer-reviewed studies arguing that fragments of a comet set it off.
At Abu Hureyra, an early village in Syria, their authors report glass melted at more than 2,200 degrees.
Then, as the cold lifts, a monument appears on a hilltop in south-east Turkey. Göbekli Tepe is a set of great rings of T-shaped stone pillars, carved with animals.
It was built around 9500 BCE, seven thousand years before the Great Pyramid.
Its excavators say the people who built it were still hunters and foragers. They had no farms, no pottery and no metal.
Its first excavator, Klaus Schmidt, believed they later filled it in on purpose.
Schoch now points to Göbekli Tepe when he is asked where the older civilisation was. For this piece too, it is what makes the rest worth taking seriously.
If people who did not farm could raise this, then a plan laid out at Giza in the eleventh millennium BCE is not absurd. It is a question of evidence.
Some of that evidence has never been gathered.
Everything so far stands on the surface. The proponents say the oldest part of Giza may lie beneath it.
In March 2025 an Italian team that includes a radar engineer, Filippo Biondi, showed what they said satellites had found under Khafre's pyramid.
Radar cannot see far into rock, and Biondi agrees. Their method reads instead the faint vibrations of the ground, the way an ultrasound reads a body.
What they read is eight hollow wells in two rows, wound with spiral paths, falling 648 metres to two great chambers about 80 metres on a side.
That is four and a half times the pyramid's height, straight down.
The rooms anyone has walked into lie three metres under its base.
Eighty kilometres south, at Hawara, stood the Labyrinth. Herodotus saw it and said it surpassed the pyramids: three thousand rooms, half of them underground, which nobody would show him.

Petrie found only a bed of stone chips, larger than the Great Pyramid's base. In 2008 Egypt's own geophysics institute surveyed the ground there, and the expedition behind it reported walls eight to twelve metres down.
Under the Sphinx's paws, Schoch's seismic survey found a hollow that has never been opened. Edgar Cayce said a Hall of Records waited there.
Nobody has dug for any of it.
Much of this case can be tested. Under the Sphinx, the test that matters most has not been made.
Look beneath the floor of the ditch. Schoch's seismic lines found the rock weathered more deeply in front of the lion than behind it.
That difference is the only measured support for the early date, and no one has tested it by drilling.
Two cores, one at the paws and one behind the rump, would show whether it is weathering, as Schoch says, or a change in the rock itself.
It can be done. In 2008 Egypt's antiquities authority and Cairo University drilled four boreholes twenty metres into the bedrock around the Sphinx, to watch the groundwater.
We have found no published record of how weathered that rock was.
Underneath, the paw cavity could be opened, the radar team could release its data, and a dig at Hawara could go below the chips.
An answer looks like this: inside the Great Pyramid, muon detectors found a hidden corridor, gave its size with error bars, and a camera confirmed it.
Hancock, Bauval and Schoch read the stone, the sky and the texts as one story. Where it has been measured, the measurements have mostly gone against it.
The ditch floor has not. Until it is, that is where to look.
